analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to have brake-shift interlocks, safer power windows, and better rear visibility to protect children.
analysis.headline: The bill became law: the House passed it by voice vote on December 19, 2007, the Senate passed it without objection on February 14, 2008, and the President signed it on February 28, 2008 (Public Law 110-189).
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Department of Transportation to write safety rules for light vehicles: power windows that reverse when they hit an obstruction, an expanded field of view behind the vehicle so drivers can see children and disabled people before backing up, and a system that requires the brake be pressed before shifting out of park to prevent rollaways. It also creates a public database of injuries and deaths in non-crash events, like backovers and children left in hot cars, and funds a public education program for parents and caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with small children, disabled people, and pedestrians near driveways and parking lots. The people most at risk from backover and rollaway incidents — small children, the elderly, and disabled people — get vehicles designed so a driver can see behind the car, windows that cannot crush a child's neck, and cars that cannot roll away when a child shifts the gear lever.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a rulemaking on power windows and panels that automatically reverse when they detect an obstruction, to prevent children from being trapped, injured, or killed [S3].

Requires a rulemaking to expand the driver's rearward field of view — through mirrors, sensors, cameras, or other technology — to reduce deaths and injuries from backing over small children and disabled persons [S6].

Requires every vehicle with an automatic transmission made after September 1, 2010 to have a system that requires the service brake to be pressed before shifting out of park, preventing rollaway incidents [S6].

Requires the Transportation Secretary to build and publish a database of injuries and deaths in nontraffic, noncrash events, and to run a consumer information program on hazards like backover incidents, hyperthermia in closed vehicles, and power window accidents [S6].

Requires manufacturers to report which models lack anti-rollaway systems and which lack auto-reversing windows, and requires the Secretary to publish that information so buyers can compare vehicles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle manufacturers, who must design and install the safety features (brake-shift interlocks, reverse-detecting windows, and rear-view technology) and report noncompliant models; those costs are generally passed into vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The costs of designing and installing the required features fall on manufacturers and are typically passed on to buyers in vehicle prices [S6].

The bill gives the Secretary discretion rather than imposing the standards outright: for power windows and rear visibility, the Secretary may determine that no additional standards are reasonable and appropriate, in which case the agency only has to report its reasons to Congress and publish which vehicles have the features [S6].
The compliance deadlines are not hard: if the Secretary determines the deadlines cannot be met, the law allows the agency to establish new deadlines after notifying Congress [S6].
Light vehicles only: motorcycles, trailers, and vehicles over 10,000 pounds are excluded, so the protections do not cover those vehicles [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted at real, documented causes of child deaths — backovers, window strangulation, and rollaways — and the anti-rollaway requirement is a hard mandate with a firm date, not a study. The main weaknesses are the escape hatches: the auto-reversing window and rear-visibility provisions leave the final decision to the Secretary, and every deadline can be extended, so the law's strength depends on follow-through by the agency.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House by voice vote, passed the Senate without objection a month later, and was signed by the President on February 28, 2008.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Janice Schakowsky on February 27, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S8].
The committee marked up the bill on December 18, 2007 and ordered it reported as amended by voice vote [S8].
On December 19, 2007, the House passed the amended bill by voice vote under a suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills [S8].
The Senate Commerce Committee was discharged from the bill by unanimous consent on February 14, 2008, and the Senate passed it without amendment the same day by unanimous consent [S8].
President George W. Bush signed the bill into law on February 28, 2008 as Public Law 110-189 [S8].
The law was named for Cameron Gulbransen, a toddler killed in a backover incident; the enacted version is titled the Cameron Gulbransen Kids Transportation Safety Act of 2007 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families and children, who gained federal safety standards for backover visibility, rollaway prevention, and power windows; automakers absorbed compliance costs but faced clear, uniform federal rules.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was broadly noncontroversial: it drew cosponsors from both parties (35 Democrats and 8 Republicans), passed the House by voice vote, and passed the Senate by unanimous consent, with no recorded opposition in the action history.

industries.note: The law requires brake-shift interlocks on all automatic-transmission cars made after September 1, 2010, and forces rulemakings on auto-reversing windows and expanded rear visibility, plus annual disclosure of noncompliant models. Manufacturers bear the design and installation costs, which are generally passed to buyers, while the safety benefit goes to the public.

industries.industry: Auto safety equipment and electronics suppliers (cameras, sensors, mirrors)
industries.note: The rear-visibility standard may be met with additional mirrors, sensors, cameras, or other technology, creating demand for suppliers of that equipment. The public benefit and the industry's gain come from the same requirement.
